mcqs.question: Why is a social post's like count a good example to defend eventual consistency with?
options: Because like counts are never actually stored in a database
Because eventual consistency is always faster than strong consistency for every field
Because like counts don't need to be accurate at all, ever
Because a brief off-by-one is unnoticeable, while synchronous global agreement on every like would add real latency for no benefit
mcqs.explanation: The case works because the cost of staleness is genuinely zero (nobody notices a momentary off-by-one) while the cost of strong consistency would be real (added latency on every single like, at massive scale). It isn't that counts are unstored or that eventual is universally faster — it's this specific cost comparison.

mcqs.question: What does "read-your-writes" consistency specifically guarantee?
options: A user who just wrote data will see that write reflected in their own subsequent reads, even while other users' reads may still be stale
All reads across all users become strongly consistent from that point forward
The write itself completes faster than it would under eventual consistency
Replicas stop diverging entirely once one user has written
mcqs.explanation: Read-your-writes is a targeted guarantee: it routes the writer's own next read to a source that has the write, without changing the consistency model for anyone else's reads. It doesn't speed up the write itself, and other replicas can still be behind.

mcqs.question: What does "bounded staleness" add that plain eventual consistency doesn't promise?
options: It guarantees zero staleness under all conditions
It removes the need for replication entirely
It converts the system to strong consistency automatically during high load
It states an explicit ceiling on how stale a read can be, such as "never more than 2 seconds behind"
mcqs.explanation: Bounded staleness is eventual consistency with a stated, enforced limit on lag — useful when "eventually" alone is too vague to design around. It doesn't eliminate staleness or replication, and it isn't a fallback that becomes strong consistency under load.

mcqs.question: A candidate assumes "eventual consistency" means replicas will always catch up within a few milliseconds. What's wrong with that assumption?
options: Nothing — a few milliseconds is the standard definition of "eventual"
Eventual consistency gives no time bound at all unless the system explicitly states one — under load or a partition, convergence can take much longer
Eventual consistency is actually a synonym for strong consistency
The assumption is wrong only for financial systems, but correct everywhere else
mcqs.explanation: "Eventual" carries no implicit time bound — that's the whole point of the term. Only an explicitly bounded-staleness design gives you a number to rely on; otherwise a slow network, backlog, or partition can stretch convergence well past milliseconds. The two models aren't synonyms, and the gap applies to any system, not just financial ones.
